This petition has been filed seeking anticipatory bail in FIR No.96/2024 dated 15th February,
2024 under Sections 420/467/468/471/34 IPC, registered at P.S. Darya Ganj.

Pursuant to the previous orders, notices have been issued on 29th July, 2024 directing the State to file a status report and, in the meantime, on the undertaking that the petitioner would join and cooperate with the investigation, interim protection was granted to the petitioner.
On the next date, the Status Report was filed by State but was not on record.
Today, when the matter had been taken up for hearing, the Status Report is on record.

Bansal Credits Limited, a Non-Banking Finance Company ["NBFC"] engaged in the business of financing of automobiles.

It was stated that, in the month of September 2020, the petitioner, along with her husband Prem Chand Sharma, approached the complainant/company and represented that she was proprietor of Shiv Motors who were authorised dealers of Piaggo Vehicles Pvt. Ltd. for Aligarh region.

On 07th September, 2020, a proposal was given on behalf of Shiv Motors that, in order to increase their sales and expand business in Aligarh, they would like to enter into a tie-up with Bansal Credits in that, while Bansal Credits will finance 3- wheeler auto-rickshaws and other commercial vehicles, the petitioner would stand as a guarantor in each of the loan agreements and take the entire liability of the guarantor.

It was further stated that since he was based in Aligarh, the verification of the borrowers would be undertaken by the firm, and the genuineness and authenticity of documents for loan agreements would be their responsibility.

On this basis, about Rs. 5.32 Crores have been disbursed with Rs.7.01 Crores receivable,
out of which, about Rs.2.39 Crores have been paid.

5. A cheque was given on 11th May, 2023 of Rs.95 Lacs signed by petitioner, which was subsequently dishonoured, and against which, proceedings under Section 138, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 have been initiated.
Upon receiving the summons in proceedings under Section 138, NI Act, a complaint was lodged by the petitioner against Bansal Credits, which seems to be done as a counter blast.

6. What was discovered later was that not only with the petitioner issued receipts on behalf of Bansal Credits, having created a letterhead of Bansal Credits, and taking monies from various borrowers, but also signing on behalf of Bansal Credits.
A couple of sample receipts have been submitted which show that the signatures on the receipts are "for Bansal Credits" by "Prop/Manager".
Clearly, this could not be executed by Bansal Credits which is a regulated NBFC and is a company.
The standard receipt issued by Bansal Credits has also been shown by APP appearing for the State.

Secondly, certain receipts which were held out by the petitioner to the borrowers represented Shiv Motors as 'AGF of Bansal Credits Ltd'. which epithet or description is not authorised by Bansal Credits.

7. It further transpired that, 70 vehicles have been repossessed by the petitioner and were found in their premises, while no such authority had been given by Bansal Credits for the same, and the repossession was completely unilateral and unauthorised.
Further, aside from the repossession of 70 vehicles, 68 other borrowers were not even traceable.
Thus, there was an issue regarding 138 borrowers.
8. As per the APP, on all these fronts, aspect of criminality arose, and the FIRs were registered.

sentences.text: Furthermore, since large amounts of monies allegedly collected by the petitioner from various borrowers, as also the vehicles are also allegedly repossessed without authority of the financing company, it does render proper investigation.

13. Reliance is also placed on the decision of the Supreme Court in State represented by the CBI v.
Anil Sharma, (1997) 7 SCC 187 in this regard, in particular the following extract:
"6.

We find force in the submission of the CBI that custodial interrogation is qualitatively more elicitation-oriented than questioning a suspect who is well ensconced with a favourable order under Section 438 of the Code.
In a case like this effective interrogation of a suspected person is of tremendous advantage in disinterring many useful information and also materials which would have been concealed.
Success in such interrogation would elude if the suspected person knows that he is well protected and insulated by a pre-arrest bail order during the time he is interrogated.
Very often interrogation in such a condition would reduce to a mere ritual.

The argument that the custodial interrogation is fraught with the danger of the person being subjected to third-degree methods need not be countenanced, for, such an argument can be advanced by all accused in all criminal cases.

The Court has to presume that responsible police officers would conduct themselves in a responsible manner and that those entrusted with the task of disinterring offences would not conduct themselves as offenders."
(emphasis added)
14.
